Chapter 33

Three languages, no library

A catalogue is an object, a message is a value or a function, and the one keyword that would collapse the whole scheme.

By the end of this chapter

Type-check every message and every argument, and express a language that has no plurals.

No message compiler, no ICU parser, no runtime interpolator. That is not minimalism for its own sake — it buys three things a runtime interpolator cannot, and the third is the one people underestimate.

The absence of as const is the most important line in that comment. With it, Messages says boards: 'Boards' — the literal — and satisfies Messages then demands that the French catalogue also say 'Boards'. Every translated line becomes a type error. Without it the strings widen to string, the function signatures are kept, and the *shape* is what is checked. Which is what we wanted to check.

Plurals in the language’s own terms

nodes: (count) => count === 1 ? '1 shape' : ${count} shapes` is not a workaround for a missing plural system. Japanese has no plural forms, and its catalogue simply does not branch — which no one{}/other{}` scheme can represent without lying, because it forces you to write the same string twice and pretend they are different cases. A function is the general form; ICU is a special case of it that happens to be data.

And the honest limit is stated too: the cost is that translators edit TypeScript. For three languages maintained by the team that writes the code, that is the right trade. It stops being right the moment translation is outsourced, and at that point these files export to JSON and the accessors stay identical.

Why these three

Chosen to cover the three shapes that break a naive interface: English as the source, French because its words are reliably longer and burst any layout measured against English, and Japanese because it has no spaces to wrap at and no plural forms at all. A fourth would be a data change — and *that* is the test of an i18n layer.

ENDONYM is never translated. A language picker in a language you cannot read is useless — somebody looking for Japanese is looking for 日本語, not for the word "Japanese" written in French.

langParam is the smallest function in the folder and the one every link uses. English is the unprefixed default — /boards, not /en/boards — so the value of the [[lang=locale]] parameter is undefined for English and the locale for everything else. The next section is why that particular shape is useful.

Quality values honoured, a bare tag matching a regional one so fr-CA finds fr, and anything unrecognised falling through to the default rather than erroring. A visitor with an exotic locale should get the app in English, not a 406.

Links that know their language

Every internal URL in Tessera — every href, and every redirect() on the server — is built with resolve() from $app/paths, never written as a string. The documentation describes it in one line: it will “resolve a pathname by prefixing it with the base path, if any, or resolve a route ID by populating dynamic segments with parameters.” The second half is the one this app leans on.

The first argument is a route id — the path of the route’s folder, [[lang=locale]] and all — and the second fills in its parameters. Pass lang: undefined and resolve() leaves the optional segment out; pass 'fr' and it puts /fr in front. So the one expression gives /boards to an English reader and /fr/boards to a French one, and langParam asks “is this the default?” once, for every link and every redirect in the app.

Why not just write the string

href="/boards" works today. It stops working the day somebody renames the folder, and nothing tells you until a person clicks it. A route id is checked against the RouteId union SvelteKit generates, so a rename breaks every link to the old route in svelte-check; the parameters are checked against that route’s own, so a missing board is a type error too; and if the app is ever served under a base path, resolve() puts it in front. The lint config enforces the habit: eslint-plugin-svelte’s no-navigation-without-resolve flags an internal href that is not a resolve() call — or a value typed as what one returns — so a hand-built link fails pnpm lint before anybody can click it.

On the server, resolve() answers with a *relative* path: in the documentation’s words, “during server rendering, the base path is relative and depends on the page currently being rendered.” That is harmless in an href and in a redirect(), which the browser resolves against the same page. It is not harmless where an absolute path is required — which is why the sign-in redirect’s from is the request’s own url.pathname, and why the sign-in form refuses any from that does not start with /.

The switcher is links

Changing language is a navigation, so the control for it is a set of links. The first version was a <select> that navigated when it changed, and that fails WCAG’s “On Input” rule in the way that hurts most: in Chromium on Windows and Linux, arrowing through a closed <select> fires change at every step, so a keyboard user heading for 日本語 was sent to Français on the first key press.

  • A <details> disclosure, so the three links take the room of one button in a crowded header, and work with no JavaScript at all.
  • resolve() with a pathname rather than a route id, because this one link has to work on whichever page it is rendered on. Written without a leading slash, which is how resolve() tells a pathname from a route id, it still comes back as a ResolvedPathname, and the lint rule is satisfied for a real reason rather than silenced.
  • data-sveltekit-reload, because the language decides what the server renders, and the client router would keep the old layout data.
  • lang and hreflang: the first so a screen reader pronounces 日本語 as Japanese, the second to say which language the page at the other end is in.
  • aria-current="page" on the language you are already reading, because that link does lead to the current page.

createContext, and the third function it returns

t was a prop. It was declared on eight components and written out at seventeen call sites, and every one of them said the same thing: *whatever my parent has*. A prop that is only ever forwarded is not a prop — it is a global with extra steps and a rename that touches eight files.

createContext arrived in Svelte 5.40, and it is not sugar for getContext. getContext('messages') is a string key and an any: two components can disagree about what is under it, a typo is a runtime undefined, and the type has to be re-asserted at every call. createContext hands back the accessors instead, so the key is a closure nobody can misspell and the type is written down once.

Three functions, and the third is the one people miss. read() returns the value or throws when no ancestor provided it — which is right, because a component that needs messages and cannot find them is broken, and a silent undefined surfaces as Cannot read properties of undefined three frames later in a component that is not the problem. provide(value) sets it. has() answers *without* throwing, which is the only way to ask whether you are inside a provider at all.

Why the context value is a function

Context is set once, at initialisation, and never again — but the catalogue is $derived(messages(data.locale)), and SvelteKit reuses a component across navigations that match the same route. Going from /boards/abc to /fr/boards/abc updates the prop in place on the component that is already mounted. Storing the catalogue would pin English forever; storing () => t stores something that genuinely never changes, and consumers wrap the call in $derived. svelte-check says so out loud if you get it wrong — "This reference only captures the initial value of t" — and it was right.

Where has earns its place

The embeddable viewer. TesseraBoard.svelte is a custom element: its own Svelte root, mounted by a page we do not control, with no ancestor of ours above it. It had three English literals in its markup — a loading line, a failure line and an aria-label — sitting outside the catalogue entirely, which is how a string stays untranslated for two years without anybody filing it.

The strict accessor cannot be used there: it throws during initialisation, and a custom element whose setup throws never defines itself at all. useMessages() asks has() first and falls back to the English catalogue — imported directly rather than through the barrel, because pulling French and Japanese into the embed bundle would undo the reason the embed exists.

That is the whole argument for has in one command. Without it the element does not render a fallback — it does not render.

The Intl cache

Intl.DateTimeFormat is expensive to construct and cheap to reuse, and a board list rebuilding one per row per render is a measurable cost on a slow phone. The cache is keyed by locale and never invalidated, because the set of locales is fixed at build time.

getOrInsertComputed, borrowed rather than called

SvelteMap has exactly this shape built in: getOrInsertComputed(key, build) reads, or builds and remembers. These two caches are deliberately not SvelteMaps, so cached is a local four-line version of it. A formatter cache is not state anything should re-render for, and reading one inside a $derived must not make that derived depend on which languages have been formatted so far — which is precisely what a reactive map would do. The name is worth having anyway: what it replaced was a get(…) ?? new … followed by an *unconditional* set, putting a write on the hot path of every timestamp on the page to re-store a value that was already there. Nobody would have noticed, which is rather the point of giving the pattern a name.

And the cut-off is a product decision worth copying: anything older than a week becomes an absolute date, because "47 weeks ago" is a number people have to convert and "12 October" is one they can read.

Checkpoint

  • A key added to English and forgotten in French fails the build.
  • Passing a string where a message wants a number fails the build.
  • Adding a fourth language touches one folder.
  • Every internal link and redirect is a resolve() call, and pnpm lint says so when one is not.
  • Switching language keeps you on the same page, and arrowing through the choices navigates nowhere.
